newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks hit by Wall St. but close above lows.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks hit by Wall St. but close above lows.

text.p: Tokyo shares closed lower on Friday but staged an impressive recovery from the depths hit in frantic morning trading after an overnight tumble on Wall Street.

Other financial markets took the New York fall calmly. The dollar was steady at about 113.20 yen, U.S. Treasury bonds ended here with modest gains and Japanese government bonds rebounded from a morning loss.
In a hectic morning session, the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares quickly fell more than 500 points, or 2.5 percent, the first time it has fallen below the key level of 20,000 in three months.

The active sell-off dragged the Nikkei down further to an intraday-low of 19,951.69 in early afternoon trading. But the market bounced back to recover a substantial chunk of its losses and the Nikkei closed the session down 159.81 points or 0.78 percent at 20,341.39
"In anticipation of pension fund buying due next week, buying emerged shortly before the market close, buoying the Nikkei average," a trader at a foreign brokerage said.

Brokers said the slumping Wall Street -- where investors are worried the recent stock rally has run its course and a downturn is due -- has dampened hopes for further blue-chip buying by foreign investors in Tokyo. This had been a pillar for the Nikkei.
"Due to the New York sell-off, we can't hope for foreign investors' buying in Tokyo. That dampened the Nikkei average," said Harushige Kobayashi, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.
The Nikkei last sank below the 20,000 level on September 3, when it marked an intraday low of 19,920.02.
New York blue-chip shares fell nearly 100 points or 1.54 percent on Thursday after a late burst of computerised programme selling in a roller-coaster session.

This was the Dow's biggest point loss since mid-July and followed a 71-point drop on Wednesday, when the market fell prey to jitters about the attractiveness of U.S. assets and fears of higher interest rates.
The outlook for Friday's opening on Wall Street was also less than rosy.

In trading on the Globex automated system, the key Standard & Poor's 500 futures contract was down five points at 729.50. Analysts calculate that the loss would equal about a 44-point drop in the Dow Jones industrial average.
Stock markets around the globe have been nervous since Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan talked a week ago about the possibility of equity markets moving too high.
The head of the U.S. central bank said that "irrational exuberance" could be affecting the markets.
World markets were also unsettled this week by fears that Japanese investors may be turning away from U.S. Treasuries, which would push up U.S. interest rates and hurt Wall Street stock prices.
Japanese government bonds (JGB) fell in early trading but the market later recovered in what analysts said was a flight to quality in the safety of government-backed securities.
The key March 10-year JGB ended at 125.05, up from 124.89.
Currency traders, meanwhile, said they saw little or no impact from the Nikkei drop.

The dollar was a shade higher than its close in New York, where it finished at around 113.17 yen. Traders said the dollar got a boost from news that European Union finance ministers agreed on a plan for budget policies under a single European currency.
U.S. Treasury securities were also little changed with the benchmark 30-year bond closing 7/32 higher at 113-3/32.
